title: Chapter 120 – Purple Mansion
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

The forty-ninth day.

Pebble wakes on the sixth day of the siege, and she is not pleased about it.

She comes out of the mist at the foot of the Reservoir stair, a small low animal the size of a loaf, armored in overlapping plates the color of wet slate, with a long tail and a blunt wedge of a snout. She has slept for four months in the damp warm hollow beside the basin, curled round herself like a cabbage, and she walks across the floor of the Dock with the weary dignity of a creature who has been robbed of something precious.

Cold, she says. The word comes into his mind like a pebble dropped in a well. Dark. Where is the sun?

"Above the wall," says Jian. He is on his knees by the bench with a ladle in his hand. "There is a war. You slept through it."

War is rude. She sniffs the Fire in its bowl, and her small black eyes widen. Hot. Hot thing. Hungry thing.

"It is a fire."

It is a mouth. She sits down on his foot, heavily, with her tail curled round her. You carry a mouth. You are a very silly boy.

He laughs, once. It is the first time in six days. He puts down the ladle and lays his hand on the cold scales of her back, and for a moment neither of them says anything, and the Dock is nearly warm.

* * *

The recipe takes forty-nine days because each fire must be taught to burn in order.

The bench lays it out on the dome in plain pale letters, and he follows it as a man follows a path across ice. Seven stations. Seven vessels, set in a ring on the long gray table. Each reagent must be brought to its own heat, held for seven days, and then passed to the next, and at the end of the seventh day the seven must be drawn together into a single crucible and taken at the hour of dawn. A mistake at any station collapses the whole. The register is quite clear about that.

The first fire is the ash.

He sets Bai's black jar on the coals of the first station and breathes on it until the lid turns red. Forty years of soot rise in a thin gray column and spread across the dome like a flower. It is the oldest fire. The one that teaches the rest to burn. He sits beside it for seven days and nights, feeding it a point a day from the Reservoir, and slowly, as it settles, he feels his own Qi go still, like a pond when the wind drops.

The second is the coral.

It lies on a bed of white sand with a corner of the Dock's cold light on it, and as the coals heat it glows from within, orange, then red, then a deep and terrible violet. It burns his skin from three feet away. He puts the Body track into it, as the register instructs, and holds the heat of it against the long ache in his bones for seven days, and when it is done his hands are blistered, his palms are cracked, and the Iron Bone he has carried since the Outer Court has changed, very slightly, in the way that a blade changes when it is quenched.

The third is silver-thread.

He cuts the plants from the Garden's east bed with his own hand, the night before the Offering, wrapped in damp cloth, and they have kept. He grinds the moon-veined leaves with Qinghe's pestle and sets them in a bowl of Reservoir water, and the water turns the color of milk and then of moonlight. He sits by it for seven days with his eyes shut. It is the Soul's fire. It does not burn. It lets go. By the end of the week he has forgotten his own name twice and remembered it each time with a small cold shock, as a man remembers where he has left a purse.

The fourth is the dew.

It sits in its green leaf-cup on a plate of clear glass, a single bead of moonlight no bigger than a pearl, and it must be kept from the lamp. He works with the Dock's light turned down to a thread. The dew drinks the dark and grows heavier, and on the third night it begins to sing, a thin high note on the edge of hearing, like a wet finger on a rim. It is the Seal's fire. When he holds his palm over it the cracked glass ring in his chest answers, and for seven days the pain that has lived there since the Gate is a pain he can hold in his hand.

The fifth is the fire-orchid, the Tan flower, with its seven red petals and its heart of white fire.

It has been kept alive in a jar of warm water since the night Ruyan handed it to him across a counting-house desk, and now it blooms. He did not know it would. One petal opens each day. By the seventh the flower has the shape of a hand with the fingers spread, and when he touches it the heat runs up his arm and into his chest in a rush, and he sees, quite clearly, a ledger page torn from a book and held out to him in the courtyard of the Garden, and Ruyan's ink-stained fingers trembling. It is the fire of debts. He pays them in his mind, one by one.

The sixth is the blood.

It must be drawn three times and tempered each time in a different flame, and each drawing costs him a measure of the soul. He cuts the inside of his left wrist with Hu's quiet knife and lets it run into a shallow bowl, and the red thing in the bowl is thick and dark and smells of iron. He heats it, and chills it, and heats it again. With the first drawing he forgets the name of the village where the Orchard stands. With the second, a song his mother used to hum. With the third, the face of a man in a white smock in a long bright corridor, a man who once, years ago, said something to him that mattered. He sits there with the bowl in his hands and tries to remember what it was, and cannot, and understands that this is the price.

He does not sleep during these. He does not dare. He eats the gray bars, one at dawn, one at dusk. He talks to Pebble, who lies by the Reservoir with her nose on her paws and tells him he is a skeleton. He listens through the floor to the dull grinding on the wall, and feels the thread of the old man in the stone thin and thicken, thin and thicken, like a heartbeat on the edge of stopping.

And each night, at the moment when he has done what he can for the day, he opens the Door in Autumn and goes up the stair and lays both hands on the granite and gives it a little more.

I will not waste it, he thinks. I will not.

* * *

Lan Tong comes through the water on the thirty-fifth day and she carries a walnut.

She steps out of the mist as before, slight and green and quiet, with the Lan leaf at her brow. She carries a small bundle of plum-colored silk in both hands. She sets it on the bench beside the Fire, and unwraps it, and inside lies a black stone the size of a thumb joint, ridged along one face with half of a key.

"She gave it to me at midnight," says Lan Tong. "At the foot of the Gate stair, under the eyes of eleven Numbers. She took it from her neck with her own hands and put it in mine. Then she walked back up the stair, and I do not know where she went."

"She is alive?"

"She was alive when I left." Lan Tong's face does not change. "She will not be for long, if the Numbers have their way. But the walnut is yours, as she promised. Not to the House. To the Dock."

Jian looks at it. Fragment three. A black, cold, quiet thing, the third part of a key that opens a door home.

He does not touch it.

"What do I do with it?"

"Nothing," says Lan Tong. "Until you must." She wraps it again with care and sets it on the shelf above the bench, beside Hu's sketches and the empty tray of Seam Needles. "It is yours. It is not an obligation. It is only a possibility."

"And if I never use it?"

"Then the Gate will stay shut, and the sleepers will sleep, and the Numbers will keep their names." She meets his eyes. "And in time the House will find another way to ask. You should know that. It will not stop asking."

"I know."

"Good." She almost smiles. "She asked me to tell you one more thing. For Ye."

"Say it."

"The stick is hers." A pause. "I never forgave myself for leaving it. I could not carry it. I thought it would be safer with her."

He closes his eyes. When he opens them she has gone, and the mist is settling, and the little walnut lies on its shelf in the lamplight like a seed.

* * *

On the forty-ninth morning, at the hour before dawn, he draws the seven fires together.

The room is silent. Even Pebble is silent, sitting upright at the foot of the stair with her black eyes unwinking. The seven vessels are lined up on the long gray table, each glowing in its own color, ash and coral and moon and dew and orchid and blood, and in the middle, a hand's breadth from the rest, in its pale blue bowl, the seventh. The Fire of the Gate has not wavered in forty-nine days. It sits quiet and gold and heavy, and when he lifts the bowl it leans against his palm like a cat.

He pours.

It goes in as a thread, bright and slow, and the other six rise to meet it. They braid. They climb. In the great crucible Bai made, under the dome, the seven colors twist together into a single column of flame, and the column changes. It narrows. It darkens. It becomes, for a moment, a deep clear violet, as of a sky seen at the edge of night, and then it falls in on itself, and where the fire was there is a single pill.

It is the size of a pea. It is the color of a plum. It sits in the bottom of the crucible and gives off a faint hum.

```
OPERATOR ARK-7 :: PURPLE MANSION PILL (SEVEN FIRES)
STATUS: COMPLETE.
COST: 90 CE. RESERVOIR 118 -> 28. CE: 9 -> 0 (FINAL TEMPERING).
SEAL: 61% -> 38% (SEVERE STRAIN). RISK OF CRACK DURING TAKING: HIGH.
ADVICE: ADVISE AGAINST. ADVISE AGAINST. ADVISE AGAINST.
```

He reads it three times.

"Pebble," he says.

Yes.

"If it goes wrong, go up the stair. Find Yue. Tell her I said she was right about the door."

What door?

"She will know."

You are a very silly boy, says Pebble, with great feeling. I am not going anywhere.

He sits down on the floor of the Dock with his back to the bench. He picks up the pill between thumb and forefinger. It is warm.

He swallows it.

* * *

It is not like the others.

The earlier breakthroughs had a sound: a hum, a bell, a rush. This has none. This is a silence so total that it has weight, a stillness like the deep of a cold lake, and he is falling through it. He is not afraid. He cannot find the part of himself that would know how. He falls past the Qi in him, vast and slow, turning like a wheel; past the Body, dense and iron-bound; past the Soul, and the small bright thing in the center of it that has been Lin Jian for thirty-six years.

And below that, in the dark, a door.

It is not a Gate. It is smaller, plainer, lower. It is a door of ordinary wood, scarred with age, standing alone in the dark with a lamp burning beside it. There is a name carved into the lintel. He knows the name. He has seen it on the register, in a field marked RESTRICTED.

Cole, Ethan.

It stands ajar.

He stops. He does not go in. He does not touch it. He only looks, and the lamp flares, and a voice speaks out of the dark behind the door, thin and dry and extremely tired, a voice with a faint accent he cannot place, speaking in a language he has not heard in thirty-six years.

Come in, it says. We have been waiting.

Then the silence closes over him like a hand.

* * *

The Purple Mansion opens above him like a sky.

It comes slowly, a circle of violet light unfolding in the dome of the Dock, and then the dome is gone and the light pours up through the stone and out through the roof of the mountain, a column of pale gold-violet fire a hundred feet across, visible to every soul in the Sect and the town and the farthest farm. It rises in a pillar into the dawn. The clouds peel back. The snow on the Gate stair goes to steam in a ring. And in the Gate Court, on the trampled ground before the wall, a hundred weary figures look up and stop.

He does not see it. He is sitting in the cold, with his eyes shut, and the Purple Mansion is a palace of nine halls inside his own chest, vast and bright and utterly silent. The three tracks stand in it side by side, Qi at the ninth step, Body at the eighth, Soul at the eighth. They are not wheels now. They are rivers. They run to a single sea.

Nine, he thinks. I am thirty-six.

Something cracks.

It is not in the Mansion. It is in the Seal. He feels it go, a long thin line of cold running across the pale glass ring in his chest, and a stab of white pain that goes through him from crown to heel. He doubles over. The Fire in its bowl gutters and blazes. The register on the wall flares and goes dark.

For a long moment nothing at all.

Then, from very far away, from above him, from the stone, comes a sound.

It is a sigh. Deep, slow, immense. It is the sound a mountain might make if it had been holding its breath for a month and had at last been told it might let go.

The wall is opening.

* * *

He comes up the stair on his hands and knees.

He does not remember deciding to. He remembers the dark, and the cold, and Pebble running ahead of him in a gray blur, and the feeling of something warm on his face that turns out to be blood. He remembers the stair being very long. Then there is light, thin, early, pearl-gray, and the smell of snow, and he is out.

The Gate Court is a field of ruin.

It lies under a low sky with the pale violet column fading above it, and the ground is littered with the wreck of a battle: broken lamp-posts, trampled banners, ash heaps where shadows have fallen, dark patches in the snow that are not shadows. A few fires burn along the edges. There are tents of the Pill Hall against the east wall. There are black-robed Law guards in a line. And there are people. Hundreds. Standing, sitting, kneeling, in the cold, with their faces turned toward the stair.

And in front of the wall, which is open, which stands apart now in two great halves like the leaves of a gate, an old man is sitting on a stool.

Qin Hao is smaller than he remembers. He is as thin as a rake, with his white beard fallen and his black cloak in tatters, and his two hands lie in his lap like objects that belong to someone else. They are the color of granite. They are quite hard. When the old man turns his head, slowly, toward the stair, his eyes are clear, and calm, and very tired, and he is smiling.

"Boy," he says. His voice is a thread. "You are late."

Jian tries to speak. He cannot. He crosses the ground between them in three steps and falls on his knees in the snow and puts his forehead against the old man's stone hands.

"Do not," says Qin Hao. "It is undignified. I am only the Elder of the Stair. I have been told I am a fixture." A dry breath. "I am afraid I cannot hold a cup any more. But I find I do not need to."

"I wasted nothing," says Jian, into the stone. "I promised."

"I know. I felt it." The old man's lips twitch. "Every point. Thirty of them. It was like a drink of warm wine."

"What happened?" he asks Qin Hao hoarsely. "Out here. In the forty-nine days."

"Oh, a great deal." The old man's voice is a thread of dry amusement. "The Numbers came at the wall for six days. They had rams. They had shadows. On the seventh, Bai brewed a jar of something he refuses to name and poured it down the stair into their ranks, and half of them were sick for a week. On the twelfth, Ye went to the Arbiter and demanded the Rule be read aloud at the gate. They read it. Twice. Three of the Numbers wept." He coughs. "On the twentieth, the Nameless stopped appearing. On the thirtieth, the House withdrew to the ridge."

"And the Keeper?"

"Has not been seen." The stone hands rest quiet in his lap. "But on the thirty-fifth night a small woman in green walked down to the foot of the stair with a bundle, and no one stopped her. I thought that was odd."

Behind Jian, there is a rush of footsteps.

* * *

His father reaches him first.

Wenyuan comes across the snow at a stumbling run, a tall stooped man with ash on his face and his sleeves burned to the elbow, and he does not say anything at all. He drops to his knees and takes his son by the shoulders and holds him at arm's length, and looks at him, up and down, in the pale light, as a man looks at a thing he had thought lost. Feng arrives a breath later. He is bleeding from a cut in his scalp, and he has the quiet blade in his hand, and he is laughing and crying and trying to say something and cannot.

"Forty-nine days," says Wenyuan hoarsely.

"Yes."

"We counted every one."

"I know."

"Your mother—" The tall man's voice breaks. "She did not sleep. She sat at the wall every night, with Yue. She would not go home."

"Where is she?"

"Here," says Qinghe.

She is standing at the edge of the crowd, small and straight in her brown shawl, with her gray-streaked hair undone and her hands folded. She does not run. She does not weep. She only looks at him across the trampled snow, and there is such a thing in her face that he has to close his eyes.

Beside her, in a robe of Sutra Hall white, her black braid pinned up like a woman's, stands Yue.

She is twenty-three. She is taller than her mother, and quieter, with her father's long jaw and eyes the gray of a river in rain. She does not look at Jian. She is looking at something on the ground at his feet. Pebble sits there, a slate-colored loaf in the snow, with her tail wrapped round her and her black eyes fixed on the girl.

And Pebble opens her mouth, and speaks.

* * *

It is not a thought. It is a voice, small and cracked and quite distinct, as of a very old child, and it carries clearly in the stillness across the Gate Court.

"Yue," says Pebble.

The girl goes white.

"I know your name. I have heard it in the dark for years." The little creature's black eyes are bright and solemn. "You sat by the door. You knew the door was there. You told him. I heard you." A pause, and a sound that might be a small hiccup. "I am Pebble. I have a message. I could not say it before. I did not have the voice."

"You can speak," whispers Yue.

"I can now." Pebble tilts her blunt head. "The mountain gave me one. Or he did. I do not know." She shuffles forward on her stubby legs and sets a small claw on the toe of the girl's boot. "He told me to say you were right about the door. I do not know what it means. But he said you would."

Yue does not speak. Tears are running down her face, silent and unchecked. She kneels in the snow, in her good white robe, and holds out both hands, and the little animal climbs into them as if she had been doing it all her life.

"I did not say it was a good door," she says unsteadily. "Only that it was there."

"It is a very strange door," says Pebble gravely. "I do not like it. But I think we are going to go through."

Ye is the last to come.

She stands at the edge of the Court with her stick planted in the snow, small and gray and entirely still, and does not approach. She has not slept in seven weeks. Her cloak is torn to the knee. Jian rises on shaking legs, with his father's hand under his elbow, and goes to her across the trampled ground, and bows, and says in a low voice that is for her alone, "She is alive. She told me to tell you the stick is yours. She says she is sorry."

Ye does not move. The wind lifts a corner of her cloak. Her pale eyes are fixed on some point behind his shoulder, very far away.

"Fifty-five years," she says at last, in a voice like dry paper.

"Yes."

"I have kept it clean." Her hand tightens on the knotted black wood. "I have oiled it every spring. I never knew whether it was a grave or a promise."

She lets him hold her arm. It is the lightest thing he has ever held.

He stands in the snow with the old woman's arm on his, his father's hand at his back and his brother at his shoulder, and the old man's stone fingers still cold against his cheek where they touched it. The sky above him is pearl-gray and very high, and a single violet thread is fading in it, like the last note of a bell. His chest is full of nine silent halls. The Seal in it is cracked from rim to rim. He feels, vaguely, that he ought to be afraid, and cannot think why.

In the pocket of his sleeve, something stirs. A line of cold text rises in his mind's eye, small and plain, and he reads it once, slowly, in the silence of the Court.

He reads the last line again, and does not breathe.

A message is waiting.
